01.note: Neḥunya, a digger of pits, ditches and caves, used to dig wells and hand them over to the public, and the Sages said he had kept this rule too. Once his daughter fell into a large cistern, and people told Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa. After the first hour he said she was at peace, after the second the same, and after the third he said she had come up. Asked who brought her up, she said a ram had come to her, led by an old man. They asked Rabbi Ḥanina whether he was a prophet; quoting Amos, he said he was not, but had reasoned that the offspring of that righteous man should not stumble through the very thing he had toiled over.
01.why: The Gemara is discussing liability for pits near the public road; a teaching that a digger who hands a well over to the public is exempt names Neḥunya as the example, and Rabbi Aḥa then adds that even so his son died of thirst.

people.name: Neḥunya
people.about: A digger of pits, ditches and caves who made wells for public use; the father of the girl who fell into the cistern.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: The Sage who was told of the girl's fall and announced, hour by hour, that she was safe and then that she had come up.

terms.meaning: A rule of Jewish law. The Sages say Neḥunya kept this one too, handing his wells over to the public.

02.note: A man was throwing stones from his own property into the public road. A pious man found him and said: Lowlife, why are you throwing stones from property that is not yours into property that is yours? The man mocked him. Some days later he had to sell his field, and while walking along that same public road he stumbled on those same stones. He said: That pious man put it well.
02.why: The story comes with the Sages' rule that a person should not clear stones from his land into the public road, part of the wider discussion of hazards people leave in public places, which the next mishna continues with pits dug there.

terms.meaning: Land open to everyone, such as a street or road, as opposed to a person's private property.

03.note: An ox fell into a water channel, and its owner slaughtered it. Rav Naḥman declared it a tereifa, an injured animal that may not be eaten. He added that if the owner had spent a kav of flour and gone to learn in the study hall, he would have known that an animal that lives a full day after such a fall is fit to eat, and he would not have lost an ox worth several kav.
03.why: The Gemara is debating whether a fall into a pit less than ten handbreadths deep can do deadly harm by impact. From this case it infers that Rav Naḥman held it can, and Rava then challenges him from the mishna.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who ruled the slaughtered ox forbidden and said the owner lost it through not knowing the law.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume. Rav Naḥman's point is that a small cost in flour would have saved an ox worth far more.
The place where the Sages and their students studied and taught the law.

04.note: Continuing his argument with Rava over the ox that fell into a water channel, Rav Naḥman says that a pit less than ten handbreadths deep is exempt when an animal dies in it because its fumes are not strong enough to kill. Rava asks how the digger can then be liable when an animal is only injured there. Rav Naḥman answers that the fumes are not enough to kill but are enough to injure.
04.why: The Gemara is testing whether Rav Naḥman's ruling on the ox fits the mishna, which exempts a shallow pit if an animal dies in it. Rava goes on to challenge him from the height of the platform used for stoning.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage defending his ruling about the ox that fell into a water channel.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who challenges Rav Naḥman's ruling from the mishna.

terms.meaning: The Gemara's word for the bad air at the bottom of a pit, thought able to kill or harm an animal that falls in.
A measure about the width of a hand. The mishna treats ten handbreadths as the depth of a pit that can kill.

04.flag: The story segment is only a legal exchange between Rav Naḥman and Rava continuing the ox case told just before it; it has no events of its own.

05.note: A man cut down another man's date palm. They came before the Exilarch, who said he had seen the place himself: three palms stood there in one cluster, worth a hundred dinars together, so the man must pay thirty-three and a third. The man said: Why should I be judged by the Exilarch, who rules by Persian law? He went to Rav Naḥman, who ruled that the damage is valued against an area sixty times larger. Rava asked Rav Naḥman whether that rule, said of damage done by a person's property, also holds for damage a person does with his own body.
05.why: The Gemara has just explained that damage to a field is valued against an area sixty times larger. Here Rav Naḥman applies that to a felled tree, and Rava's question opens the debate that follows on damage done directly by a person.

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: The judge who first heard the case and valued the palm as a third of the cluster.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage the man turned to, who valued the damage against an area sixty times larger.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who questioned whether Rav Naḥman's rule applies to damage done by a person himself.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who also acted as a judge.
A silver coin.

06.note: Eliezer Ze'eira was standing in the market of Neharde'a wearing black shoes. Officials of the Exilarch's house asked why, and he said he was mourning Jerusalem. Thinking it presumptuous, they put him in prison. He said he was a great scholar and offered to prove it, and they told him to ask. He asked what someone who cuts the flower cluster of another's date palm must pay, and knocked down each answer they gave. Asked for his own answer, he said the damage is valued against an area sixty times larger, and told them Shmuel and his court could confirm it. They sent to Shmuel, who said he was right, and they released him.
06.why: The Gemara has been weighing how to value a damaged date palm, setting the sixty-times rule against the Exilarch's approach. In this story Shmuel himself confirms the sixty-times rule.

people.name: Eliezer Ze'eira
people.about: A scholar jailed for wearing black shoes in mourning for Jerusalem, who won his release by a legal question.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose court was asked, and who confirmed Eliezer Ze'eira's ruling.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia; here his officials have the power to arrest and release.

07.note: Rabban Gamliel blinded the eye of his slave Tavi and was overjoyed, because a slave whose master blinds his eye goes free. He met Rabbi Yehoshua and asked: Do you know that my slave Tavi has gone free? Rabbi Yehoshua asked why, and Rabban Gamliel said: Because I blinded his eye. Rabbi Yehoshua told him his words meant nothing, since there were no witnesses.
07.why: Rav Huna, citing Rav, holds that a man who admits to an act carrying a fine stays exempt even if witnesses come later. Rav Ḥisda cites this case against him: it implies that with witnesses Rabban Gamliel would have had to free Tavi despite admitting it first.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Tavi's master, who blinded his slave's eye and was glad of it.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's Canaanite slave.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who told Rabban Gamliel that without witnesses his admission did not free Tavi.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reports Rav's ruling that admitting to a fine exempts a person even if witnesses come later.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Raises this incident as an objection to Rav Huna.

terms.meaning: A payment the Torah sets as a penalty rather than as repayment of an actual loss. Freeing a slave whose eye was blinded is treated as one, and a fine is not imposed on a person's own admission.
A non-Jewish slave held by a Jewish master.

08.note: A pious man was suffering from pain in his heart. The physicians said his only remedy was to suckle warm milk every morning, so a she-goat was brought and tied to the leg of his bed. Days later his friends came to visit, saw the goat, and turned back, saying: There is an armed bandit in this man's house, and we are going in to him? They looked into his conduct and found no sin but the goat, and at his death he himself said it was his only sin, because he had gone against the words of his colleagues.
08.why: Rabban Gamliel has just allowed keeping such an animal for a while only if it is tied to the legs of the bed and does not graze with the flock. The pious man did just that, yet the story still counts it as his one sin.

09.note: A woman's son was causing her grief, and she jumped up and swore: Any man who comes to marry me, I will not turn away. Unworthy men jumped at the chance. When the matter came before the Sages, they said she had meant only a man suited to her.
09.why: The teaching just before says a man who vowed to buy a house or marry a woman in the Land of Israel need not take the first one he finds but may wait for one suited to him. This incident reads a woman's oath the same way.

10.note: Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, said that in Babylonia they had taken on themselves the Land of Israel's ban on raising sheep and goats. Rav Adda bar Ahava asked Rav Huna about his own animals. Rav Huna said his wife Ḥova watched over them. Rav Adda bar Ahava said: May Ḥova bury her son! For all the years of Rav Adda bar Ahava's life, no children of Rav Huna by Ḥova survived. Another version says the ban took hold in Babylonia only from the time Rav came there.
10.why: The baraita under discussion bans raising small domesticated animals in the Land of Israel. This exchange asks whether the ban also binds Jews in Babylonia, and how strictly.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage cited as saying Babylonia took on the Land of Israel's ban.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports Rav's statement about the ban in Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: Challenges Rav Huna over his animals and curses his wife's children.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Keeps sheep and goats, saying his wife Ḥova guards them.

people.name: Ḥova
people.about: Rav Huna's wife, who watched over his animals.

terms.meaning: Sheep and goats. The Sages banned raising them in the Land of Israel.
The Land of Israel.

11.note: Rav, Shmuel and Rav Asi came to a celebration for a newborn son (some say for the redemption of a firstborn). None would go in ahead of another: Rav not before Shmuel, Shmuel not before Rav Asi, Rav Asi not before Rav. They decided Shmuel would wait while Rav and Rav Asi went in. The Gemara explains that Rav deferred to Shmuel only as a gesture, because of an incident in which he had cursed him. Meanwhile a cat came and severed the baby's hand. Rav went out and taught that a cat may be killed, may not be kept, and is protected neither by the laws of theft nor by the duty to return lost property.
11.why: The baraita being discussed lists animals one may or may not raise, and one view allows cats because they clear houses of vermin. Rav's ruling after this incident forbids keeping one, and the Gemara goes on to reconcile the two.

people.name: Rav
people.about: One of the three Sages at the celebration; after the cat attack he ruled against keeping cats.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: One of the three Sages, who stayed behind so the others could enter.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The third Sage; he would not go in before Rav.

terms.meaning: A celebration for a newborn boy; the translation takes it as a circumcision.
A ceremony in which a father redeems his firstborn son from a priest with a payment.

12.note: Rabbi and Rabbi Ḥiyya were walking on a road and stepped off to its sides. Ahead of them, Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa was taking long strides along the road itself. Rabbi asked who this was, showing off his greatness before them. Rabbi Ḥiyya said it might be his student Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa, all of whose actions were for the sake of Heaven. When they reached him and Rabbi saw him, he said: If you were not Yehuda ben Kanosa, I would have cut off your legs with iron shears.
12.why: The Gemara is going through Joshua's conditions for the land, one of which lets travelers step off a rough road onto private land. Here great Sages use that right, and Rabbi treats passing it up as a show of pride.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, walking with Rabbi Ḥiyya; he took the man ahead for a show-off.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Rabbi's companion, who said the man was probably his own student.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa
people.about: Rabbi Ḥiyya's student, who kept to the road instead of stepping off it.

terms.meaning: Done out of real devotion to God rather than for one's own glory.

13.note: When the Hasmonean royal house was at war with itself, Hyrcanus was inside Jerusalem and Aristobulus outside. Each day those inside lowered coins in a box, and those outside sent up animals for the daily offerings. An elder there who knew Greek wisdom told the besiegers that as long as the Temple service went on, the city would not be handed over to them. The next day, when the coins came down, they sent up a pig. When it reached the middle of the wall it dug its hooves in, and the Land of Israel quaked over four hundred parasangs by four hundred. At that time the Sages said: Cursed is the man who raises pigs, and cursed is the man who teaches his son Greek wisdom. A mishna records that in that time the barley and wheat for two Temple offerings had to come from distant places.
13.why: The mishna rules that no one may raise pigs anywhere, and this account is given as the background to that rule. The Gemara then asks whether Greek wisdom is really forbidden.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: The Hasmonean who was inside besieged Jerusalem.

people.name: Aristobulus
people.about: The Hasmonean besieging Jerusalem from outside.

terms.meaning: The Jewish royal family that ruled the Land of Israel; here two of its members are at war.
The sacrifices brought in the Temple every morning and afternoon.
Greek learning; the Sages cursed whoever taught it to his son.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles long.

14.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, applying a verse from Lamentations, said there had been a thousand children in his father's household: five hundred studied Torah and five hundred studied Greek wisdom, and of them only he and his cousin in Asia Minor remained. The Sages, the Gemara adds, allowed Avtolmos bar Reuven to cut his hair in the Roman komi style, normally forbidden, because he was close to the government, and for the same reason allowed Rabban Gamliel's household to study Greek wisdom.
14.why: The Sages have just cursed anyone who teaches his son Greek wisdom. The Gemara tests that against sayings praising the Greek language and against Rabban Gamliel's household, answering that language differs from wisdom and that this family was a special case.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Tells of the thousand children of his father's household, of whom only he and a cousin remained.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's father, whose household studied Greek wisdom.

people.name: Avtolmos bar Reuven
people.about: A man allowed the Roman haircut because he was close to the government.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Says that in Babylonia one should speak Hebrew or Persian rather than Aramaic.

terms.meaning: Greek learning, as distinct from the Greek language; the Sages restricted the first but not the second.
A haircut in a style favored by the Romans.
Gentile customs that the Torah forbids Jews to copy.

14.flag: The story segments open mid-sentence (Rabbi's statement begins in the segment before) and are mostly the Gemara's back-and-forth over Greek wisdom; the only narrative is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's brief report and the ruling for Avtolmos.

15.note: A woman went into a house to bake, and a dog barked at her. Its owner told her not to be afraid, since its canine teeth had been removed. She answered: Take your favors and throw them on the thorns! The baby has already moved.
15.why: Rabbi Dostai has just taught that a dog that frightens a pregnant woman into miscarrying can drive the Divine Presence from Israel. This incident shows a dog doing that harm even without its teeth, within the discussion of restrictions on raising dogs.

16.note: A donkey severed a child's hand, and the case came before Rav Pappa bar Shmuel. He told the court officers to assess four types of payment. Rava objected that the mishna lists five; Rav Pappa bar Shmuel said he meant besides the damage itself. Abaye objected that a donkey's owner pays only for damage, so he told them to assess the damage. Asked whether the child had to be valued as a slave, he said yes. The child's father refused, saying it would demean the boy. Told he was acting against the child, he said that when the boy grew up he would appease him with his own money.
16.why: The Gemara has just discussed how an injured person's loss is measured, including whether the court values him as if he were a slave. This case puts that method into practice, and a similar case before Rava follows.

people.name: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel
people.about: The judge in the case of the child's severed hand.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects that the mishna lists five types of payment, not four.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects that a donkey's owner pays only for the damage itself.

terms.meaning: The mishna's list of what someone who injures a person must pay: the damage, pain, medical costs, lost time and humiliation.
Measuring an injury by how much it would lower a person's price if he were sold as a slave.

17.note: The mother of Rav Shmuel bar Abba of Hagroneya, who was married to Rabbi Abba, signed her property over to her son. After she died, Rav Shmuel bar Abba went to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba, who confirmed him as owner. Her husband, Rabbi Abba, took the matter to Rav Hoshaya, who brought it to Rav Yehuda; Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel that a husband can take back property his wife sold in his lifetime. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba answered from a mishna about a father who signs property over to his son, and Rav Yehuda replied, again citing Shmuel, that this case is not like that mishna. The text does not say who finally kept the property.
17.why: The case becomes a test of whether owning the right to a property's produce counts as owning the property itself, the point Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish dispute. Afterward Rav Yosef and Abaye argue over why Shmuel set the two cases apart.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Abba
people.about: The son to whom his mother signed over her property.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: His mother's husband, who contested the gift.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: The judge who confirmed the son as owner and defended his ruling from a mishna.

people.name: Rav Hoshaya
people.about: Brought Rabbi Abba's complaint to Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Cited Shmuel's rulings against the son's claim.

terms.meaning: Property a wife owns while her husband has the right to its produce and income.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

18.note: In the mishna's incident, a man uncovered a woman's head in the marketplace, and Rabbi Akiva made him pay her for the humiliation. Given time to pay, the man waited until she stood at the door of her courtyard and got her to uncover her own head. The Gemara asks how he could be given time, when Rabbi Ḥanina says no time is given for injuries, and answers that humiliation, unlike injury, causes no money loss. It then cites a baraita in which Rabbi Akiva told the man: You dived into mighty waters and came up with a potsherd in your hand, for a person may injure himself.
18.why: The Gemara has been asking whether humiliation payments are scaled to the victim's standing; Rabbi Akiva holds that even the poor deserve full payment. His case is then tested against other rulings on time to pay and on harming oneself.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who made the man pay for humiliating the woman.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Says the court gives no time to pay for injuries.

terms.meaning: One of the payments owed for harming someone: compensation for the shame caused.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

18.flag: The story segments name the mishna's incident only by its opening words with 'etc.' and are mostly the Gemara's questions about it; the events are filled in by the translation.

19.note: A man slaughtered an animal or bird, and someone else got there first and covered its blood. Rabban Gamliel ruled that the second man must pay the slaughterer ten gold coins.
19.why: Rav has just explained a claim for payment of the form 'I wanted to do this commandment myself.' A baraita teaches that the one who slaughters must cover the blood, and this case is the precedent for paying a man who was robbed of that commandment.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who made the man who covered the blood pay the slaughterer.

terms.meaning: The Torah's command that whoever slaughters a wild animal or bird must cover its blood with dust.

20.note: Shmuel's sharecropper brought him dates, and Shmuel tasted wine in them. He asked why, and the sharecropper said the palms stood among the grapevines. Shmuel said: Do they weaken the vines that much? Tomorrow bring me from their marrow, meaning cut the palms down.
20.why: The Gemara has just taught when a fruit tree may be cut down despite the ban on destroying trees. Shmuel's order to fell palms that drew strength from more valuable vines is a case in point, and Rav Ḥisda does the same just after.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The landowner who tasted wine in his dates and had the palms cut down.

terms.meaning: A farmer who works another's land in return for a share of the crop.
The soft heart of a palm, which can be taken only by cutting the tree down.
